tracks.name: Frontend system design
tracks.blurb: The frontend system design round: design a product's client architecture in 45 minutes with RADIO, from feeds and chat to collaborative editors and spreadsheets.

lessons.title: How to answer frontend system design (RADIO)
lessons.summary: The RADIO framework, a 45-minute time plan, the questions to ask, component trees, state placement and API choices, with a worked example.
lessons.body:
## What this round actually is
A frontend system design interview asks you to design the **client architecture** of a product in about 45 minutes: "design a news feed", "design autocomplete", "design Google Docs". The backend is a black box you negotiate an API with. The interviewer wants to see how you break a vague product into components, where state lives, what crosses the network and how you keep it fast, accessible and robust.

It is not a coding round and not a backend scaling round. Spending ten minutes on database sharding is a classic way to fail it. Spending ten minutes on CSS colours is the other way.

## The RADIO framework
A widely used structure (popularised by GreatFrontEnd) is **RADIO**:

| Step | Question it answers | Rough time |
|---|---|---|
| **R**equirements | What are we building, for whom, at what scale? | 5-8 min |
| **A**rchitecture | Which components exist and how do they talk? | 8-10 min |
| **D**ata model | What entities live on the client, and in which store? | 5-8 min |
| **I**nterface | What is the API between client and server (and between components)? | 5-8 min |
| **O**ptimisations | Performance, accessibility, i18n, offline, security, edge cases | 10-15 min |

Say the framework out loud at the start ("I'll clarify requirements, sketch the architecture, then data, API, and spend most time on optimisations"). It shows structure and lets the interviewer steer.

## Requirements: the questions to ask
Split them into functional and non-functional. Write them down where the interviewer can see.

**Functional** (what the user can do):
- Core flows only. For a feed: view posts, create a post, like, comment. Agree to leave out ads, stories and DMs.
- Which content types? Text, images, video, polls?
- Real-time or refresh-based?

**Non-functional** (how well):
- Devices: desktop only, mobile web, both? Low-end Android on 3G?
- Scale on the client: how many items in a list, how big is a document, how many concurrent collaborators?
- Offline support needed?
- Accessibility and internationalisation (RTL languages)?
- SEO: does the page need to be indexed? That decides SSR vs CSR.

A good habit: state an assumption when the interviewer says "you decide". "I'll assume mobile web matters and the feed can be thousands of posts long, so virtualisation is in scope."

## Architecture: draw the component tree
Draw boxes for the major parts: views, the client store, the network layer, and the server. Keep it to 6-10 boxes.

```text
+--------------------------- Browser ----------------------------+
|                                                                |
|  App shell (router, layout, auth context)                      |
|    |                                                           |
|    +-- FeedPage                                                |
|    |     +-- Composer        +-- FeedList (virtualised)        |
|    |                               +-- PostCard x N            |
|    |                                                           |
|  Client store (normalised entities + request cache)            |
|    ^            |                                              |
|    | updates    | reads                                        |
|  Data layer: API client, retries, dedupe, optimistic updates   |
|    |                       ^                                   |
+----|-----------------------|-----------------------------------+
     v HTTP (REST/GraphQL)   | push (SSE/WebSocket)
  +--------------------- Server / BFF -----------------------+
```

Explain the responsibility of each box in one sentence. The important separation is **views vs data layer**: views render from the store; the data layer owns fetching, caching, retries and real-time updates. This is the shape of TanStack Query, Apollo, Relay and RTK Query.

## Data model and state placement
List the entities and their fields as TypeScript interfaces. Then decide **where each piece of state lives**:

| Kind of state | Where | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Server cache | Data layer / query cache | posts, users, comments |
| Shared UI state | Global store or context | current user, theme, unread count |
| Local UI state | Component state | is the menu open, input text |
| URL state | Router / search params | active tab, filters, selected item |
| Persistent client state | IndexedDB / localStorage | drafts, offline queue |

```ts
interface User { id: string; name: string; avatarUrl: string }
interface Post {
  id: string;
  authorId: string;          // reference, not an embedded User
  text: string;
  media: Media[];
  likeCount: number;
  likedByMe: boolean;
  createdAt: string;         // ISO 8601
}
interface FeedState {
  postIds: string[];         // order of the feed
  nextCursor: string | null;
  status: "idle" | "loading" | "error";
}
```

Normalising (posts reference `authorId`) means one user's name change updates every post. Put filters and selected ids in the URL so refresh and share work.

## Interface: the API
Pick the transport per interaction, and justify it:

- **REST** for simple resources and when HTTP caching (CDN, ETag) helps.
- **GraphQL** when screens need data from many resources and you want one round trip with exactly the fields you render; costs: tooling, caching is harder at the HTTP layer.
- **SSE** for server-to-client streams (notifications, live scores, LLM tokens).
- **WebSocket** for low-latency two-way traffic (chat, collaboration, games).

Write the endpoint and its shapes:

```ts
// GET /api/feed?cursor=abc&limit=20
interface FeedResponse {
  posts: Post[];
  users: Record<string, User>;   // side-loaded authors, avoids N+1 on the client
  nextCursor: string | null;
}

// POST /api/posts/:id/like   body: { clientMutationId: string }
interface LikeResponse { postId: string; likeCount: number; likedByMe: boolean }
```

Mention pagination style (cursor), error shapes and idempotency keys for mutations.

## Optimisations: where senior candidates separate
Pick the 4-5 that matter most for this product rather than reciting a checklist:

- **Performance:** code splitting by route, virtualised long lists, image `srcset` and lazy loading, prefetch on hover, skeletons, avoiding layout shift (reserve space with `aspect-ratio`).
- **Network:** request dedupe, caching with stale-while-revalidate, batching, retries with exponential backoff and jitter.
- **Accessibility:** semantic HTML, keyboard paths, focus management, ARIA patterns for custom widgets, `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- **i18n:** externalised strings, `Intl` formatting, RTL via logical CSS properties.
- **Offline / resilience:** service worker caching, IndexedDB queue, optimistic UI with rollback.
- **Security:** XSS (never inject user HTML; sanitise rich text), CSRF on cookie auth, CSP, rate-limit friendly clients.

## A worked mini example: "Design a like button"
In two minutes, the whole framework:

1. **R:** toggle like, show count, works on a feed of 1,000 posts, fast on mobile, accessible.
2. **A:** `LikeButton` reads `post.likedByMe` and `likeCount` from the store and calls `toggleLike(postId)` in the data layer.
3. **D:** fields live on the normalised `Post`; no local copy, so every view of the post stays in sync.
4. **I:** `PUT /posts/:id/like` and `DELETE /posts/:id/like` (idempotent, so retries are safe) instead of a "toggle" endpoint that flips state twice on a retry.
5. **O:** optimistic update with rollback on error, debounce rapid double clicks, `aria-pressed` on the button, count formatted with `Intl.NumberFormat` compact notation.

## What interviewers score
- **Problem exploration:** did you ask questions and scope it?
- **Architecture:** sensible components and separation of concerns.
- **Technical depth:** real knowledge of browser APIs and trade-offs, not buzzwords.
- **Breadth of optimisations:** performance, a11y, i18n, offline, security.
- **Communication:** you drive, check in, and adapt when steered.

## Common mistakes
- Jumping into React code or CSS before requirements.
- Designing the backend (database choice, sharding) in depth.
- One giant global store for everything, including input text.
- Listing optimisations without tying them to the product's constraints.
- Not leaving 10+ minutes for optimisations, where most senior signal comes from.

## In the interview
Open with the plan, write requirements, draw the tree, show interfaces in TypeScript, then go deep on 3-4 optimisations. Check in every 10 minutes: "Is there an area you'd like me to go deeper on?" When challenged, name the trade-off and pick one; indecision scores worse than a defended choice.
keyPoints: RADIO: Requirements, Architecture, Data model, Interface, Optimisations; say the plan out loud first
Spend 10-15 minutes on optimisations: performance, a11y, i18n, offline and security are where senior signal comes from
Separate views from a data layer that owns fetching, caching, retries and real-time updates
Place state deliberately: server cache, global UI, local UI, URL, persistent client storage
Pick REST, GraphQL, SSE or WebSocket per interaction and justify it with the product's needs
interview: Walk me through how you structure a 45-minute frontend system design interview.
How do you decide where a piece of state lives in a large client application?
When would you pick REST, GraphQL, SSE or WebSockets for the client-server interface?

check.q: Fifteen minutes into a 'design a news feed' round you are discussing database sharding. What is the best correction?
options: Keep going, backend depth always impresses
Bring it back to the client: components, client store, API shape and optimisations
Switch to writing the React components in full
Ask the interviewer to pick the database
check.why: This round scores client architecture. The backend is a black box you agree an API with; deep backend design spends time without earning signal.

check.q: Where should the active filter and selected tab of a search results page usually live?
check.why: URL state survives refresh, can be shared and works with back/forward. Component or global state loses it.

check.q: Why prefer PUT /posts/:id/like plus DELETE over POST /posts/:id/toggle-like?
options: PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so a retried request cannot flip the state twice
Toggle endpoints are not allowed in REST
check.why: Network retries happen. An idempotent set/unset produces the same result however many times it is sent; a toggle retried once undoes itself.

lessons.title: Design a news feed (Facebook / Twitter)
lessons.summary: Infinite scroll with IntersectionObserver, cursor pagination, virtualisation, optimistic likes, a new-posts banner, lazy media and the ARIA feed pattern.
keyPoints: Cursor pagination keeps pages stable while new posts arrive; offset pagination repeats or skips items
Observe a sentinel with IntersectionObserver and a large rootMargin instead of listening to scroll
Virtualise long, variable-height lists; content-visibility is a cheaper first step
Optimistic likes: update the normalised store, call an idempotent endpoint, reconcile or roll back
Never insert new posts above the reader; show a 'new posts' pill and use role=feed with articles
interview: Design a news feed like Facebook or Twitter for the web.
Cursor-based vs offset-based pagination: which do you use for an infinite-scrolling UI and why?
How do you implement optimistic UI for likes and comments, and how do you roll back on failure?

check.q: A user scrolls a live feed using ?page=N pagination while 5 new posts are published. What happens on the next page?
options: The next page repeats about 5 posts the user already saw
check.why: Inserts at the top shift every item down by 5, so the next offset window overlaps the previous one. A cursor anchored to the last seen item avoids this.

check.q: Which image in a feed should NOT have loading="lazy"?
options: The first post's image visible on load
check.why: The first visible image is often the LCP element. Lazy loading delays it; give it eager loading and fetchpriority=high instead.

check.q: Why store posts normalised (by id) instead of embedding copies in each list?
options: It uses less CPU to render
One update (like count, author name) is reflected everywhere the entity appears
check.why: Each entity exists once, lists hold ids, so a change in one place updates the feed, the modal and the profile view together.

lessons.title: Design typeahead / autocomplete
lessons.summary: Debounce, AbortController cancellation, stale-response guards, an LRU cache with TTL, keyboard navigation and the ARIA combobox pattern.
keyPoints: Debounce reduces requests; cancellation plus a stale-query check fixes out-of-order responses
Cache results per normalised query in a bounded LRU with a TTL
Focus stays in the input; aria-activedescendant points at the highlighted option
Render highlighted matches as React text segments, never as injected HTML
Ship it as a headless hook so teams can bring their own data source and item rendering
interview: Design an autocomplete / typeahead search component.
How do you prevent race conditions when typing quickly fires several search requests?

check.q: The 'ip' request returns after the 'iph' request and overwrites its results. Which fix fully solves this?
options: Abort the previous request and ignore responses whose query is not the current one
check.why: Debounce only reduces the chance. Cancelling plus discarding stale responses guarantees the UI shows the latest query's results.

check.q: In the ARIA combobox pattern, where is DOM focus while the user arrows through suggestions?
options: In the text input, with aria-activedescendant identifying the active option
check.why: Focus stays in the input so typing keeps working; aria-activedescendant tells assistive tech which option is active.

check.q: Why use onMouseDown with preventDefault on suggestion items?
options: It prevents the input's blur from closing the list before the click registers
It is required for touch screens
It stops the request from being sent
check.why: mousedown fires before blur; preventing the default keeps focus in the input so the popup is still there when the selection happens.

lessons.title: Design a chat app (WhatsApp / Messenger web)
lessons.summary: WebSocket lifecycle and reconnect, ordering by server sequence, idempotent client ids, receipts, an IndexedDB outbox, presence and a bottom-anchored list.
lessons.body:
## The problem
"Design WhatsApp Web or Facebook Messenger." The user has a list of conversations and an open thread; messages arrive in real time, sent messages show sent/delivered/read ticks, typing indicators appear, and the app survives a flaky connection. It tests real-time transport, ordering, idempotency, offline storage and a list that scrolls the "wrong" way.

## Requirements
**Functional:** conversation list with unread counts and last message; open a thread and load history; send text (and images); receipts (sent, delivered, read); typing indicator and online presence; group chats.

**Non-functional:** messages appear in under a second, never duplicated or lost, correct order, works offline (read history, queue outgoing), smooth with threads of 10,000+ messages, accessible, multi-tab safe.

## Architecture
```text
ChatApp
 +-- ConversationList (virtualised, sorted by lastMessageAt)
 +-- ThreadView
 |     +-- MessageList (virtualised, anchored to bottom, loads older on scroll up)
 |     +-- TypingIndicator
 |     +-- Composer -> sendMessage()
 +-- ConnectionBanner ("Reconnecting...")

Data layer
 +-- SocketClient (connect, heartbeat, reconnect with backoff, resubscribe)
 +-- MessageStore (normalised, by conversation, sorted by server sequence)
 +-- Outbox (IndexedDB queue of unsent messages)
 +-- Persistence (IndexedDB cache of conversations and recent messages)
```

The UI never talks to the socket directly. Events flow socket -> store -> views; user actions flow views -> outbox -> socket.

## Data model
```ts
type MessageStatus = "pending" | "sent" | "delivered" | "read" | "failed";

interface Message {
  clientId: string;          // uuid generated on the device, the idempotency key
  id?: string;               // server id, assigned on ack
  conversationId: string;
  senderId: string;
  body: string;
  seq?: number;              // server-assigned, monotonic per conversation
  createdAt: string;         // client time, for display while pending
  status: MessageStatus;
}

interface Conversation {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  memberIds: string[];
  lastMessageAt: string;
  unreadCount: number;
  lastReadSeq: number;       // my read pointer
}
```

## Interface: WebSocket messages
```ts
type ClientEvent =
  | { type: "send"; clientId: string; conversationId: string; body: string }
  | { type: "read"; conversationId: string; upToSeq: number }
  | { type: "typing"; conversationId: string }
  | { type: "sync"; cursors: Record<string, number> };       // after reconnect

type ServerEvent =
  | { type: "ack"; clientId: string; id: string; seq: number }
  | { type: "message"; message: Message }
  | { type: "receipt"; conversationId: string; userId: string; kind: "delivered" | "read"; upToSeq: number }
  | { type: "typing"; conversationId: string; userId: string }
  | { type: "presence"; userId: string; online: boolean; lastSeen?: string };
```

History uses plain HTTP: `GET /conversations/:id/messages?beforeSeq=1200&limit=50`.

### Why WebSocket here
Chat is bidirectional, frequent and latency-sensitive: typing events, receipts and messages both ways. A WebSocket gives one long-lived full-duplex connection. SSE is server-to-client only (you would POST sends), which works but doubles the paths. Long polling is the fallback for hostile networks. Note: serverless platforms such as Vercel functions cannot hold WebSockets, so you use a dedicated realtime service.

## Connection lifecycle and reconnect
```text
 CONNECTING --open--> OPEN --close/error--> WAITING(backoff) --timer--> CONNECTING
      ^                 |                                                  |
      |                 +-- heartbeat missed --> close ---------------------+
      +--------------- online event / tab visible: retry now --------------+
```

- **Heartbeat:** send a ping every ~25 s; if no pong in time, treat the socket as dead (TCP can stay "open" while the network is gone).
- **Exponential backoff with jitter:** wait `min(30s, base * 2^attempt) * random(0.5..1)`, so a server restart does not get a thundering herd of reconnects.
- Listen to `online`/`offline` and `visibilitychange` to reconnect immediately when it makes sense.
- **On reconnect, resync:** send the last `seq` you have per conversation; the server replays what you missed. Then flush the outbox.

## Ordering and idempotency
Client clocks are wrong and messages from several senders interleave, so **order by server sequence**, not by client timestamp. The server assigns `seq` per conversation on accept.

Retries happen (socket drops after send, before ack). The **clientId** makes sends idempotent: the server stores it and returns the same ack for a duplicate instead of creating a second message. The client merges by `clientId`, so a message that arrives both as an ack and as a broadcast is stored once.

```ts
function upsertMessage(m: Message) {
  const existing = byClientId.get(m.clientId);
  byClientId.set(m.clientId, { ...existing, ...m });
  // keep the conversation array sorted by seq; pending messages (no seq) stay at the end
}
```

## Receipts, typing and presence
- **Sent:** server ack received. **Delivered:** the recipient's device received it (it sends a delivered receipt). **Read:** the recipient viewed the thread. Send read receipts as a **watermark** ("read up to seq 1200"), not per message: one event instead of hundreds.
- **Typing:** throttle to one event every ~3 s while typing; the receiver hides the indicator after ~5 s without a new event. Never persist typing.
- **Presence:** online/last seen, fanned out only to contacts with an open chat to limit traffic. Respect privacy settings.

## Offline queue in IndexedDB
On send: write the message to the IndexedDB outbox with status `pending`, render it immediately, then try the socket. On ack, mark it `sent` and remove it from the outbox. On reload or reconnect, replay the outbox in order. After N failures mark it `failed` with "Tap to retry".

Cache conversations and the last ~100 messages per thread in IndexedDB so the app opens instantly offline. With multiple tabs, elect one tab to own the socket (Web Locks API or a `BroadcastChannel` leader) or use a SharedWorker, otherwise each tab opens its own connection and receipts double.

## Message list anchored to the bottom
Chat scrolls upward: new messages at the bottom, history loads when scrolling up.

- If the user is at the bottom, new messages keep it pinned to the bottom. If they scrolled up to read, do not yank them; show "3 new messages" instead.
- Prepending older messages must **preserve scroll position**: record the distance from the bottom (`scrollHeight - scrollTop`) before prepending and restore it after layout (`useLayoutEffect`). CSS `overflow-anchor` helps in some browsers but is not supported in Safari, so do it explicitly.
- Virtualise with a library that supports reverse lists and variable heights (react-virtuoso has this built in).
- Accessibility: the thread is a `role="log"` region (implicitly polite live region) so new messages are announced; each message has sender and time in its accessible name.

## End-to-end encryption awareness
In WhatsApp (Signal protocol), messages are encrypted on the device; the server routes ciphertext it cannot read. Frontend consequences: keys live on the device (IndexedDB, ideally non-extractable WebCrypto keys), each linked device has its own keys, server-side search and link previews are impossible (the client generates previews), and push notifications carry no plaintext. You are not expected to design the crypto; you are expected to know where it changes the client design.

## Other optimisations
- Render message text as text; auto-link URLs as tokens. Sanitise any rich content.
- Image upload: show a local blob preview at once, upload in the background with progress, and send the message referencing the uploaded media id.
- Batch store updates arriving in bursts (one render per animation frame).
- Notifications: the Notification API when the tab is hidden, plus a title badge.

## Common mistakes
- Sorting by client timestamps.
- Retrying sends without an idempotency key, producing duplicates.
- Reconnecting immediately in a tight loop with no backoff.
- Forgetting to resync missed messages after a reconnect.
- Per-message read receipts and unthrottled typing events.

## In the interview
Sketch socket -> store -> views, write the event types, then go deep on three things: reconnect with backoff and resync, ordering by server seq plus clientId idempotency, and the bottom-anchored virtual list. Mention the outbox and multi-tab leader election to show production awareness.
keyPoints: Heartbeats detect dead sockets; reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, then resync missed messages
Order by server-assigned sequence, never client clocks; dedupe by a client-generated id
Read receipts as a watermark (read up to seq N); throttle typing events
Write outgoing messages to an IndexedDB outbox first, render as pending, flush on reconnect
Keep the message list pinned to the bottom and preserve scroll position when prepending history
interview: Design a chat application like WhatsApp Web or Messenger.
WebSocket vs Server-Sent Events vs long polling: how do you choose?
How do you guarantee message ordering and avoid duplicates when the client retries?

check.q: Why add random jitter to reconnect backoff delays?
options: To avoid every client reconnecting at the same instant after a server restart
check.why: Without jitter, thousands of clients retry on the same schedule and overload the server in waves (thundering herd).

check.q: A send's ack is lost and the client retries. How does the server avoid storing the message twice?
options: It deduplicates on the client-generated message id (idempotency key)
check.why: The clientId uniquely identifies the send attempt; the server returns the existing ack for a repeated id instead of creating a new message.

check.q: What is the main reason not to sort chat messages by the sender's device timestamp?
options: Device clocks drift and differ, so concurrent messages can appear in the wrong order
check.why: Clocks across devices are not synchronised. A server-assigned per-conversation sequence gives every client the same order.

lessons.title: Design a collaborative editor (Google Docs / Figma)
lessons.summary: OT vs CRDTs (Yjs, Automerge), awareness and presence cursors, per-user undo, offline merge, document model, permissions and large-document performance.
lessons.body:
## The problem
"Design Google Docs" or "design Figma's multiplayer". Several people edit the same document at the same time, see each other's cursors, keep working offline and never lose an edit. The hard part is **concurrency**: two users change the same place at the same moment, and every client must end up with the same document.

## Requirements
**Functional:** rich-text editing, real-time co-editing, remote cursors and selections with names, comments, version history, share with view/comment/edit permissions, offline editing that merges on reconnect.

**Non-functional:** local keystrokes apply in under one frame (never wait for the network), convergence (all replicas end identical), documents of 100+ pages, tens of concurrent editors, undo that only undoes your own changes.

## Architecture
```text
Editor UI (ProseMirror / Lexical / Slate view)
   |  local transactions                ^ remote changes applied
   v                                    |
Document model (CRDT doc or OT client: pending + sent ops)
   |                       |                         |
   | updates               | awareness               | persist
   v                       v                         v
Sync provider (WebSocket)  Presence (cursors, names) IndexedDB (offline copy)
   |
Server: relay + authority (OT transform / CRDT merge), snapshots, permissions, history
```

Key principle: the local document is the source of truth for rendering; the network only exchanges operations.

## Document model
Represent the document as a **tree** (paragraphs, headings, lists, text runs with marks), not an HTML string. Editors like ProseMirror and Lexical use a schema-validated tree with positions; operations are "insert text at position", "add mark bold to range", "split block".

```ts
interface DocNode { type: "doc" | "paragraph" | "heading" | "list_item"; attrs?: Record<string, unknown>; content: (DocNode | TextNode)[] }
interface TextNode { type: "text"; text: string; marks: ("bold" | "italic" | "link")[] }

interface Awareness {           // ephemeral, never stored in the doc
  user: { id: string; name: string; color: string };
  cursor: { anchor: RelativePosition; head: RelativePosition } | null;
}
```

## OT vs CRDT
Both solve "Alice and Bob edited concurrently; make every replica converge".

**Operational Transformation (OT)** - Google Docs' approach. Operations are index-based (`insert "x" at 5`). When two operations are concurrent, a transform function adjusts one against the other: if Alice inserts 3 characters at position 2 and Bob deletes position 10, Bob's delete is transformed to position 13. A **central server** orders operations and is the authority; each client keeps "sent but unacknowledged" and "pending" ops and transforms incoming ops against them.

```text
Alice: ins(2,"abc")  --\        server orders: A then B
Bob:   del(10)       ---\-->    B transformed: del(13)
                              all clients apply A, del(13) -> same doc
```

**CRDTs** (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) - Yjs, Automerge. Every character (or run) gets a unique id (client id + counter) and is positioned relative to its neighbours' ids, not indexes. Merge is commutative, associative and idempotent, so replicas converge regardless of order or duplication, **without a central authority**. Deletes leave tombstones (Yjs compacts them aggressively).

| | OT | CRDT |
|---|---|---|
| Server | Required, orders and transforms | Optional; any relay or peer-to-peer |
| Offline | Hard: long divergence means big transforms | Natural: merge whenever you reconnect |
| Correctness | Transform functions are notoriously hard to get right | Convergence guaranteed by construction |
| Memory | Small: plain document | Metadata per item (Yjs is very compact) |
| Used by | Google Docs, older Etherpad | Yjs (many editors), Automerge, Figma-style custom approaches |

Figma uses its own server-authoritative scheme inspired by CRDTs (last-writer-wins per property for objects), because design objects are mostly properties, not long text sequences. In 2026, for a new product, the pragmatic choice is usually **Yjs** with an editor binding (y-prosemirror, Lexical's Yjs plugin, Tiptap Collaboration) and a WebSocket provider.

## Interface
```ts
// WebSocket, binary frames (Yjs updates are compact Uint8Array)
type SyncMessage =
  | { type: "sync-step-1"; stateVector: Uint8Array }  // "here's what I have"
  | { type: "sync-step-2"; update: Uint8Array }       // "here's what you're missing"
  | { type: "update"; update: Uint8Array }            // incremental change
  | { type: "awareness"; states: Uint8Array };        // cursors, names

// REST
// GET  /docs/:id            -> { title, role: "viewer" | "commenter" | "editor", snapshotUrl }
// GET  /docs/:id/versions   -> named snapshots for history
// POST /docs/:id/share      -> { userEmail, role }
```

The state-vector handshake means a client reconnecting after a day offline sends only what the server lacks and receives only what it lacks.

## Presence and awareness
Cursors, selections and "who's here" are **awareness** state: ephemeral, broadcast frequently, never written into the document. Cursor positions must be **relative positions** (anchored to a CRDT item id), not integer offsets, otherwise a remote insert above shifts everyone's cursor to the wrong place. Throttle awareness updates (for example every 50-100 ms) and remove a user's state after a timeout when they disconnect.

## Undo in multiplayer
Global undo would revert someone else's typing. Undo must be **per user**: track only your own operations and invert them against the current document. Yjs's `UndoManager` does this by tracking transactions with a local origin; it also groups keystrokes typed within a short window into one undo step.

## Offline edits and merge
Persist the CRDT document in IndexedDB (y-indexeddb). Offline edits apply locally; on reconnect the sync handshake exchanges missing updates and the merge is automatic. Semantic conflicts can still exist (two people rewrote the same sentence differently: both edits survive interleaved), so offer version history and highlight recent changes rather than pretending conflicts never happen.

## Permissions
Enforce on the server: a viewer's socket receives updates but the server drops any update it sends. The UI also sets the editor read-only and hides tools, but that is convenience, not security. Comments can be a separate data structure anchored to relative positions so they survive edits.

## Performance of large documents
- Keep keystroke handling local and synchronous; batch outgoing updates (send every ~50 ms or per transaction).
- Store periodic **snapshots** server-side so new clients load a snapshot plus recent updates, not the whole history.
- Render only visible pages for very long docs (Google Docs moved to canvas-based rendering for layout control; most editors use virtualised or `content-visibility` blocks).
- Lazy-load heavy features (comments panel, history) and run expensive work such as word count or spell check off the main thread.

## Common mistakes
- Sending the whole document on every change.
- Storing cursors as integer offsets.
- Global undo that reverts collaborators' work.
- Treating client-side read-only mode as permission enforcement.
- Claiming CRDTs remove the need for a server: you still need auth, persistence and fan-out.

## In the interview
Clarify text vs canvas objects, draw the editor - doc model - provider - server pipeline, explain OT vs CRDT with a two-user example, then pick one and defend it. Go deep on awareness with relative positions, per-user undo, offline merge and snapshots. Expect: "What happens if two users bold and delete the same word?" and "How do you load a 200-page doc fast?"
keyPoints: OT transforms index-based operations through a central server; CRDTs give every item an id so merges converge in any order
Local edits apply instantly; the network only exchanges operations or updates
Cursors are ephemeral awareness state anchored to relative positions, not integer offsets
Undo must be per user: only invert your own operations
Enforce permissions on the server; snapshots plus recent updates make big docs load fast
interview: Design a collaborative document editor like Google Docs.
Explain OT vs CRDTs. Which would you pick for a new collaborative product?

check.q: Which property makes CRDTs well suited to offline editing?
options: They require a central server to order operations
Merges are commutative and idempotent, so replicas converge regardless of order or duplication
They store the document as HTML
They lock paragraphs while someone edits
check.why: Because merge order does not matter, a client can edit offline for hours and merge on reconnect without a transform step.

check.q: Why store remote cursors as relative positions rather than integer offsets?
options: Integers are too small for long documents
An insert earlier in the doc shifts integer offsets, so cursors would point at the wrong place
check.why: A relative position is anchored to an item id, so it stays attached to the same character as the document changes around it.

check.q: Alice presses Ctrl+Z after Bob typed a sentence. What should happen?
options: Alice's last own change is undone; Bob's text stays
Nothing, undo is disabled in multiplayer
The whole document reverts to the last snapshot
check.why: Multiplayer undo is scoped to the local user's operations, as Yjs's UndoManager does with tracked origins.

lessons.title: Design an image gallery and video player
lessons.summary: srcset and sizes, AVIF/WebP, CDN resizing, lazy loading and blur-up placeholders, HLS/DASH adaptive streaming with MSE, and resumable chunked uploads.
lessons.body:
## The problem
"Design an image gallery like Google Photos or Unsplash" or "design the YouTube player". Media is usually the heaviest thing on a page, so this round is about bytes: which file each device downloads, when, and how to make it feel instant. Uploads are the other half: large files on unreliable connections.

## Requirements
**Functional:** grid of thumbnails with infinite scroll; open a lightbox with swipe/arrow navigation; play video with quality switching; upload photos and videos with progress, pause and resume.

**Non-functional:** fast LCP on mobile, no layout shift, minimal data on cellular, smooth 60 fps scrolling, keyboard and screen-reader support, uploads survive network drops and page reloads.

## Architecture
```text
GalleryPage
 +-- MediaGrid (virtualised rows, justified or masonry layout)
 |     +-- Thumb x N (responsive img, blur-up placeholder, lazy)
 +-- Lightbox (dialog) -> preloads next/prev full images
 +-- VideoPlayer (MSE + HLS/DASH via hls.js / dash.js / Shaka, or native HLS on Safari)
 +-- Uploader -> UploadQueue (chunked, resumable, IndexedDB-backed)

CDN image service: /img/:id?w=640&fmt=auto  (resize + AVIF/WebP negotiation)
Object storage <- presigned multipart upload URLs
```

## Data model
```ts
interface Photo {
  id: string;
  width: number;             // original dimensions, to reserve aspect ratio
  height: number;
  blurhash: string;          // ~20-30 char placeholder
  dominantColor: string;
  takenAt: string;
  alt: string;
}

interface Upload {
  id: string;                // client id
  file: File;                // kept in IndexedDB so it survives reloads
  uploadId?: string;         // server multipart session
  chunkSize: number;         // e.g. 5-8 MB
  completedParts: number[];
  status: "queued" | "uploading" | "paused" | "done" | "error";
  bytesSent: number;
}
```

## Interface
```ts
// GET /api/photos?cursor=...&limit=60 -> { photos: Photo[]; nextCursor: string | null }
// Image URL built on the client: `${CDN}/img/${id}?w=${w}&q=75` (format chosen by the CDN from Accept)

// Resumable upload
// POST /api/uploads            { filename, size, mime } -> { uploadId, chunkSize }
// PUT  presignedUrl(part n)    raw bytes                -> ETag
// GET  /api/uploads/:id        -> { completedParts }     // resume after reload
// POST /api/uploads/:id/complete { parts }              -> { photo: Photo }
```

## Responsive images
The browser should pick the right file; you describe the options.

```tsx
const WIDTHS = [320, 640, 960, 1280];

function thumbProps(p: Photo): ImgHTMLAttributes<HTMLImageElement> {
  return {
    src: cdn(p.id, 640),
    srcSet: WIDTHS.map((w) => `${cdn(p.id, w)} ${w}w`).join(", "),
    sizes: "(max-width: 600px) 50vw, (max-width: 1200px) 33vw, 300px",
    width: p.width,
    height: p.height,
    loading: "lazy",
    decoding: "async",
    alt: p.alt,
  };
}
// rendered as an img element spreading thumbProps(photo)
```

- `srcset` with `w` descriptors plus `sizes` (how wide the image will render) lets the browser factor in viewport and device pixel ratio.
- **Formats:** AVIF is typically smaller than WebP, which is smaller than JPEG, at similar quality. Either serve via `picture` with `type` sources, or let the CDN negotiate from the `Accept` header (`fmt=auto`), which keeps markup simple.
- **CDN resizing:** never ship a 4000px original to a 300px slot. Image CDNs (Cloudinary, imgix, Cloudflare Images, Next.js `next/image`) resize on the fly and cache each variant at the edge. Limit allowed widths to a fixed set so the cache stays hot and nobody can request 10,000 variants.

## Lazy loading and placeholders
- Native `loading="lazy"` for everything below the fold; **eager** with `fetchpriority="high"` for the first visible image (likely LCP).
- Width/height attributes or `aspect-ratio` reserve space, so no CLS.
- **Blur-up:** render the blurhash (or a tiny 20px JPEG, or the dominant colour) as the background, then fade in the real image on load. Users perceive progress instead of grey boxes.
- In the lightbox, **preload** the next and previous full-size images (`new Image().src = url`, or `link rel=preload` for the very next), and decode before showing (`img.decode()`) so swipes do not flash.

## Grid layout and virtualisation
A justified layout (Google Photos, Flickr) computes rows from aspect ratios so every row fills the width; this needs the dimensions from the API before images load. With tens of thousands of photos, virtualise by row: only rows near the viewport are in the DOM. Google Photos also computes section heights from counts so the scrollbar is accurate before loading everything.

## Video: adaptive bitrate streaming
A single MP4 forces one quality. **Adaptive bitrate (ABR)** streaming splits the video into short segments (2-6 s) encoded at several bitrates (a "ladder", e.g. 240p to 4K). A manifest lists them:

- **HLS** (`.m3u8`) - Apple's; plays natively in Safari and iOS.
- **DASH** (`.mpd`) - the ISO standard; played in other browsers via JavaScript.

```text
 manifest.m3u8
   240p  400 kbps  -> seg_240_001.ts, seg_240_002.ts ...
   720p  2.5 Mbps  -> seg_720_001.ts ...
   1080p 5 Mbps    -> seg_1080_001.ts ...

 Player loop: measure throughput + buffer level -> choose next segment's rendition
              -> fetch -> append to SourceBuffer (MSE) -> video element plays
```

Outside Safari, the player uses **Media Source Extensions (MSE)**: JavaScript fetches segments and appends them to a `SourceBuffer` attached to a `video` element. hls.js, dash.js and Shaka Player implement the ABR logic. They start low for a fast first frame, then climb as bandwidth allows, and drop before the buffer runs dry. DRM uses EME on top.

Player UX details interviewers like: poster image, preload metadata only until play, keyboard shortcuts (space, arrows, M, F), captions via `track` (WebVTT), remembered position, thumbnail previews on the seek bar (a sprite sheet), Picture-in-Picture, and `prefers-reduced-motion` respected for autoplay.

## Upload flow: chunked and resumable
A 2 GB video over mobile will fail at some point. So:

1. Ask the server to start a **multipart upload**; get an upload id and presigned URLs per part (S3 multipart parts are at least 5 MB except the last).
2. Slice the file with `file.slice(start, end)` and upload 3-4 parts in parallel.
3. Track progress per part (`XMLHttpRequest.upload.onprogress`, since `fetch` has no upload progress events in most browsers) and sum them for a smooth bar.
4. On failure, retry that part with backoff; the rest stay done.
5. Persist the queue (File objects can be stored in IndexedDB) so a reload resumes: ask the server which parts exist, upload the rest.
6. Complete the upload; the server transcodes asynchronously and notifies when the video is ready.

Generate a client-side preview immediately (`URL.createObjectURL(file)`) and resize/compress images in the browser (canvas or `createImageBitmap`) before uploading to save bandwidth. Strip EXIF location data unless the user opts in.

## Accessibility
Lightbox is a modal `dialog` with focus trap and focus return to the thumbnail; arrows navigate; Escape closes. Every image needs meaningful `alt` (AI-generated alt text with user editing is a good answer). Video needs captions and keyboard-operable controls with labels.

## Common mistakes
- Lazy-loading the hero image, hurting LCP.
- No dimensions, so the grid jumps as images arrive.
- Unbounded CDN resize parameters.
- Uploading big files in one request with no resume.
- Autoplaying video with sound.

## In the interview
Start from bytes: which variants exist, how the browser chooses, when they load. Then the grid (dimensions from API, virtualisation), the lightbox preloading, ABR with HLS/DASH and MSE, and the resumable upload state machine. Quantify: "a 300px slot at 2x DPR needs a ~600px image, maybe 40 KB as AVIF instead of 2 MB."
keyPoints: Describe options with srcset and sizes and let the browser choose; a CDN resizes and negotiates AVIF/WebP
Reserve space from known dimensions; lazy-load below the fold but prioritise the LCP image
Blur-up placeholders and preloading the next lightbox image make media feel instant
ABR streaming: segmented renditions in an HLS or DASH manifest, fed to the video element through MSE
Large uploads are chunked, parallel, retried per part and resumable after a reload
interview: Design an image gallery that loads fast on slow mobile networks.
Design a video streaming player like YouTube's for the web.

check.q: What does the sizes attribute tell the browser?
options: The file size of each candidate image
How wide the image will be rendered at different viewport widths
check.why: Combined with srcset w descriptors and the device pixel ratio, sizes lets the browser pick the smallest adequate file before layout.

check.q: In Chrome, how does an HLS player such as hls.js get video segments into the video element?
options: Fetches segments and appends them to a SourceBuffer via Media Source Extensions
check.why: Safari plays HLS natively; elsewhere JavaScript players fetch segments, choose renditions and append them through MSE.

check.q: Why upload a 2 GB video in chunks instead of one request?
options: Servers reject large requests by law
A failure only retries one chunk, parts can go in parallel, and the upload can resume after a reload
check.why: On mobile networks a single long request will likely fail; chunking makes progress durable and retries cheap.

lessons.title: Design a large data table / spreadsheet
lessons.summary: 2D virtualisation, sticky panes, client vs server sort, cell editing, a formula dependency graph with topological recalculation, workers, the ARIA grid and clipboard.
lessons.body:
## The problem
"Design a data table with 100,000 rows" (admin panels, trading blotters, Airtable) or "design Google Sheets". Rendering every cell would create millions of DOM nodes, so the core is **2D virtualisation**. Spreadsheets add a formula engine: cells depend on other cells, and changing one must recalculate exactly the cells that depend on it, without freezing the UI.

## Requirements
**Functional:** scroll a large grid smoothly; sticky header row and first column; sort, filter and resize columns; edit cells inline; keyboard navigation like Excel; copy/paste ranges with other apps; for spreadsheets, formulas such as `=SUM(A1:A10)*B2`.

**Non-functional:** 60 fps scrolling with 100k rows x 50 columns, edits feel instant, recalculation never blocks typing, accessible to screen readers, copy/paste interoperable with Excel and Google Sheets.

## Architecture
```text
GridView
 +-- HeaderRow (sticky top)   +-- RowHeaders (sticky left)
 +-- Viewport (one scroll container)
 |     +-- VisibleCells only (rows r0..r1 x cols c0..c1 + overscan)
 +-- CellEditor (single input positioned over the active cell)
 +-- SelectionLayer (active cell, ranges, copy marquee)

Data layer
 +-- RowModel: data source -> filter -> sort -> view index (client or server)
 +-- CellStore: Map of "r:c" -> { raw, value, format }
 +-- FormulaEngine (Web Worker): parser, dependency graph, recalculation
```

## Data model
```ts
type CellId = `${number}:${number}`;          // "row:col"

interface Cell {
  raw: string;               // what the user typed: "42" or "=A1*2"
  value: number | string | boolean | null | { error: "#REF!" | "#DIV/0!" | "#CYCLE!" };
  format?: { numFmt?: string; bold?: boolean };
}

interface Column { id: string; title: string; width: number; type: "text" | "number" | "date"; pinned?: "left" }

interface ViewState {
  sort: { colId: string; dir: "asc" | "desc" }[];
  filters: Record<string, string>;
  scroll: { top: number; left: number };
  selection: { anchor: CellId; focus: CellId };
}
```

Spreadsheets are **sparse**: store only non-empty cells in a Map, never a 2D array of a million entries.

## Interface
```ts
// Table with server-side data
// GET /api/rows?offset=40000&limit=200&sort=price:desc&filter=status:open
//   -> { rows: Row[]; total: number }           // offset is fine for a fixed, sorted snapshot

// Spreadsheet sync
// PATCH /api/sheets/:id/cells  { changes: { id: CellId; raw: string }[], baseVersion: number }
// Worker messages
type ToWorker = { type: "set"; changes: { id: CellId; raw: string }[] };
type FromWorker = { type: "values"; updates: { id: CellId; value: Cell["value"] }[] };
```

For random-access scrolling over a huge server dataset, offset/limit windows (or row-index ranges) suit grids better than cursors, because the user can drag the scrollbar to row 73,000 directly.

## 2D virtualisation
Compute the visible window from scroll position and sizes, render only those cells, absolutely positioned inside a container sized to the full grid.

```ts
function visibleRange(scrollTop: number, viewportH: number, rowH: number, total: number, overscan = 5) {
  const first = Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / rowH) - overscan);
  const last = Math.min(total - 1, Math.ceil((scrollTop + viewportH) / rowH) + overscan);
  return { first, last };
}
// Same for columns, but widths vary: keep prefix sums of widths and binary-search scrollLeft.
```

```text
 full content size: 100k rows x 32px = 3,200,000 px tall (inner spacer)
 +------------------------------------------+
 | header (sticky)                          |
 |   rendered: rows 1200..1240 x cols 3..14 |  <- ~500 cells in the DOM
 +------------------------------------------+
```

Details that matter:
- **Fixed row height** makes math O(1); variable heights need measured sizes and prefix sums.
- Browsers cap element height (around 16-33 million px depending on engine), so for many millions of rows you scale scroll positions or use a custom scrollbar.
- **Recycle** cell components by position keys to avoid mount/unmount churn; update with `transform: translate` rather than `top` for cheaper compositing.
- At extreme scale (Google Sheets, Excel Online) cells are drawn on a **canvas**, with a DOM overlay for the editor and an accessibility layer, because canvas rendering avoids per-cell DOM cost.

## Sticky headers and columns
`position: sticky` on the header row (`top: 0`) and pinned columns (`left: 0`) inside the single scroll container keeps scrolling synchronised for free. Using separate scroll containers forces JS scroll syncing, which lags by a frame and looks broken.

## Sorting and filtering: client or server
| Data size | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Under ~10-50k rows already loaded | Client | Instant, no round trip; do it in a worker if it takes over ~50 ms |
| Larger or not fully loaded | Server | The client cannot sort what it has not downloaded |

Sort a **view index** (array of row ids), never the underlying data, so you can unsort and keep edits stable. Locale-aware string sort: `Intl.Collator`.

## Cell editing
One editor input, positioned over the active cell, rather than an input in every cell. Enter or typing starts editing, Enter commits and moves down, Tab moves right, Escape cancels. Commit applies optimistically to the store and queues a sync; validation errors show inline on the cell.

## Formula engine
1. **Parse** `=SUM(A1:A3)*B2` into an AST (tokeniser plus a recursive-descent or Pratt parser handling precedence, ranges, function calls, absolute refs like `$A$1`).
2. **Dependency graph:** for each formula cell, record the cells it reads (precedents) and invert it so each cell knows its dependents.
3. **Recalculate** when a cell changes: collect all transitive dependents, **topologically sort** them, and evaluate in order so each cell computes after its inputs.
4. **Cycle detection:** if the topological sort cannot finish (Kahn's algorithm leaves nodes with non-zero in-degree, or DFS finds a back edge), mark those cells `#CYCLE!`.

```text
 A1 = 5      B1 = A1 * 2      C1 = A1 + B1
 change A1 -> dirty {B1, C1} -> topo order: B1, C1 -> evaluate
```

Only recalculating dirty dependents (not the whole sheet) is what keeps edits fast in 100k-cell sheets.

## Web Workers
Parsing, recalculation, sorting and CSV parsing run in a **Web Worker** so the main thread stays free for scrolling and typing. Send only changed values back, batched. Transferable objects (ArrayBuffers) avoid copying large data. The UI shows a subtle "calculating" state if results lag.

## Keyboard navigation and the ARIA grid pattern
- `role="grid"` with `role="row"`, `role="columnheader"`, `role="gridcell"`; `aria-rowcount`/`aria-colcount` give the **total** size and `aria-rowindex`/`aria-colindex` the position of each rendered cell, so screen readers understand a virtualised grid.
- **Roving tabindex:** one cell has `tabIndex=0`, all others -1; Tab moves into and out of the grid, arrows move within it.
- Keys: arrows, Home/End, Ctrl+Home/End, Page Up/Down, Shift+arrows to extend selection, F2 or Enter to edit.
- When navigation goes beyond the rendered window, scroll first, then focus the newly rendered cell.

## Copy and paste
Listen to `copy`/`paste` events on the grid. On copy, write the selection as **TSV** (`text/plain`, tabs between cells, newlines between rows), which Excel and Sheets understand, plus optionally `text/html` with a table. On paste, parse TSV from `clipboardData`, write the values starting at the active cell and grow the selection. The async Clipboard API (`navigator.clipboard`) needs permissions and focus; the events are more reliable.

## Common mistakes
- Rendering all rows, or a 2D array for a sparse sheet.
- Separate scroll containers for frozen panes.
- Recalculating the whole sheet on every edit.
- Running the formula engine on the main thread.
- An input in every cell, and no roving tabindex.

## In the interview
Draw viewport plus overlays, show the visible-range math, then choose client vs server sort by data size. For Sheets, walk the parse - graph - topo sort - cycle pipeline with the A1/B1/C1 example, and move it into a worker. Close with the ARIA grid pattern and TSV clipboard.
keyPoints: Render only the visible window of rows and columns inside one scroll container sized to the full grid
Sticky header and pinned columns with position: sticky avoid JavaScript scroll syncing
Sort and filter on the client below tens of thousands of loaded rows, otherwise on the server
Formulas: parse to AST, build a dependency graph, recalc dirty dependents in topological order, flag cycles
Use role=grid, aria-rowcount/rowindex for virtualised rows, roving tabindex and TSV copy/paste
interview: Design a data table that renders 100,000 rows smoothly.
Design a spreadsheet like Google Sheets in the browser.

check.q: A1=5, B1=A1*2, C1=A1+B1. The user changes A1. In what order must cells be recalculated?
check.why: C1 depends on B1, so a topological order of the dirty dependents evaluates B1 first, then C1.

check.q: How should a virtualised grid tell screen readers its true size?
options: aria-rowcount and aria-colcount on the grid plus aria-rowindex and aria-colindex on rendered cells
Use a live region announcing the count on every scroll
check.why: These attributes describe the full dimensions and each rendered cell's position even though most cells are not in the DOM.

check.q: Which clipboard format pastes cleanly into Excel and Google Sheets as a range?
options: Tab-separated values with newlines between rows
check.why: Spreadsheets read text/plain TSV from the clipboard as a grid of cells; an HTML table is an optional richer flavour.

projects.title: Real-time collaborative whiteboard
projects.summary: A multiplayer whiteboard like a small Excalidraw or FigJam: draw shapes and freehand strokes on a canvas, see other people's cursors live, keep working offline, undo your own changes and share a room with a link.
projects.why: It is the frontend system design round built for real: CRDT-based sync, presence, offline persistence, per-user undo and a canvas renderer that stays at 60 fps. Few portfolios show a working answer to 'design Figma'. You can demo it live with two browser windows, and every design decision maps to a classic interview follow-up.
projects.architecture:
```text
Browser (per user)
  React UI: Toolbar, RoomHeader, ShareDialog
  CanvasStage
    static layer canvas (committed shapes, redrawn on change)
    live layer canvas (in-progress stroke, selection, remote cursors)
  Y.Doc
    shapes: Y.Map of id -> Y.Map(shape props)
    order:  Y.Array of ids (z-order)
  UndoManager (tracks local origin only)
  Awareness (cursor, name, colour, selection)
  y-indexeddb (offline copy)   y-websocket provider
                                   |
Node server: y-websocket rooms, auth token per room, periodic snapshot to disk/S3
```

Key decisions: shapes as a Y.Map keyed by id with per-property maps, so concurrent edits to different properties of the same shape both survive; z-order as a separate Y.Array. Two canvases so a moving cursor never forces a full redraw. Presence lives in awareness, never in the document. The server is a dumb relay plus persistence; convergence comes from the CRDT.

milestones.title: Single-user canvas
details: Rectangle, ellipse, arrow, text and freehand tools drawn on a 2D canvas with devicePixelRatio scaling
Pan and zoom with a view transform; hit-testing to select and move shapes
Checkable: draw 500 shapes and pan at 60 fps in the Performance panel

milestones.title: Document model in Yjs
details: Store shapes in a Y.Map of Y.Maps and z-order in a Y.Array; render from the Y.Doc via an observer
Batch each drag into one transaction so it is one update and one undo step
Checkable: reload the page with y-indexeddb and the drawing is still there

milestones.title: Real-time sync
details: y-websocket server with rooms; client connects with the room id from the URL
Show connection state and reconnect automatically
Checkable: two browsers draw simultaneously and converge to identical drawings

milestones.title: Presence
details: Awareness with name, colour and cursor in canvas coordinates, throttled to about 20 updates per second
Render remote cursors and selections on the live layer; remove stale users after a timeout
Checkable: cursors move smoothly and disappear when a tab closes

milestones.title: Undo, redo and offline
details: Y.UndoManager scoped to the local origin; Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z
Go offline in DevTools, draw, come back online and verify both sides merge
Checkable: undo never removes another user's shape

milestones.title: Rooms, sharing and export
details: Create room, copy share link with a view or edit token; server rejects updates from view tokens
Export PNG (canvas.toBlob) and SVG (serialise shapes)
Checkable: a view-only link can watch but not change the board

milestones.title: Performance, accessibility and write-up
details: Spatial index or bounding-box culling so only visible shapes are drawn
Keyboard shortcuts for tools, a screen-reader list of shapes, and reduced motion
Write up measured frame times, update sizes and sync latency in the README

stretch: Infinite canvas with tiles and level-of-detail rendering
WebRTC peer-to-peer provider as an alternative transport
Smart shapes: connectors that follow when shapes move
resume: Built a real-time collaborative whiteboard with Yjs CRDTs and WebSockets, supporting [N] concurrent editors with median sync latency of [X ms]
Kept rendering at [Y] fps with [Z] shapes by splitting static and live canvas layers and culling off-screen shapes
Implemented offline editing with IndexedDB persistence and conflict-free merge on reconnect, plus per-user undo/redo
Reduced sync payloads by [P%] by batching drag operations into single CRDT transactions
talking: Why I chose a CRDT (Yjs) over OT, and what the server still has to do
How per-property Y.Maps let two users change colour and position of the same shape concurrently
Why presence is awareness state and not part of the document
How two canvas layers avoid full redraws when cursors move
How per-user undo works in a shared document
features: Draw rectangles, ellipses, arrows, text and freehand strokes on an infinite pannable, zoomable canvas
Live multiplayer editing with named, coloured remote cursors and selections
Works offline; changes merge automatically when the connection returns
Undo and redo that only affect your own changes
Share links with view-only or edit access
Export the board as PNG or SVG

deepDives.title: Why CRDTs over OT, and how to model shapes
Rendering at 60 fps with two canvas layers
deepDives.body:
The DOM (or SVG) approach creates a node per shape; with thousands of shapes and constant cursor movement, style and layout costs dominate. A 2D canvas draws everything in one immediate-mode pass, but naive redraws on every pointer move still burn the frame budget.

**Split the work:**

```text
static canvas : committed shapes; redraw only when the doc changes or the view pans/zooms
live canvas   : in-progress stroke, selection handles, remote cursors; redraw every frame while active
```

Remote cursors move 20 times per second per user; on the live layer that costs a handful of draw calls instead of redrawing every shape.

**Render loop:** observers on the Y.Doc mark the static layer dirty; a single `requestAnimationFrame` loop redraws dirty layers once per frame, so a burst of 50 remote updates becomes one redraw.

**Crisp output:** size the backing store by `devicePixelRatio` and scale the context, otherwise lines look blurry on high-DPI screens.

```ts
canvas.width = cssWidth * dpr; canvas.height = cssHeight * dpr;
ctx.setTransform(dpr * zoom, 0, 0, dpr * zoom, -panX * dpr, -panY * dpr);
```

**Culling:** keep each shape's bounding box; skip shapes outside the viewport. For very large boards, a spatial index (a simple grid of buckets or an R-tree such as rbush) makes both culling and hit-testing fast.

**Freehand strokes:** sample pointer events with `getCoalescedEvents()` for smoothness, simplify points (Ramer-Douglas-Peucker) before committing to the doc to keep updates small, and render with quadratic curves.

**Measure:** record a Performance trace while dragging with two remote users and report frame times in the README.

deepDives.title: Per-user undo and offline merge
Presence and cursors with the awareness protocol

projects.title: Browser spreadsheet with a formula engine
projects.summary: A Google Sheets-style app in the browser: a virtualised grid with 100k+ cells, formulas with a hand-written parser, a dependency graph with topological recalculation and cycle detection running in a Web Worker, plus keyboard navigation, copy/paste and CSV import/export.
projects.why: It proves computer-science depth inside a frontend: a parser, graph algorithms, incremental computation, worker messaging and 2D virtualisation, all measurable. It is the exact answer to 'design Google Sheets' and gives you numbers to talk about (cells, recalculation time, frame rate) rather than adjectives.
projects.architecture:
```text
Main thread
  GridView
    header row + row numbers (position: sticky)
    viewport: visible window of rows x cols (2D virtualised)
    CellEditor overlay, selection layer, formula bar
  SheetStore: Map of "r:c" -> { raw, value, format }  (sparse)
  Clipboard (TSV), CSV import/export, IndexedDB autosave
        |  postMessage({ type: "set", changes })
        v
Worker: FormulaEngine
  tokenizer -> Pratt parser -> AST cache per cell
  dependency graph (precedents / dependents, range index)
  dirty set -> Kahn topological sort -> evaluate -> cycle cells marked #CYCLE!
        |  postMessage({ type: "values", updates })  (only changed cells)
        v
Main thread applies updates in one batch per frame
```

Key decisions: a sparse Map instead of a 2D array; the engine lives entirely in a worker so typing and scrolling never block; recalculation touches only transitive dependents of the edited cells; ranges are indexed as ranges rather than expanded into thousands of edges.

deepDives.title: Writing the formula parser
Dependency graph, topological recalculation and cycles
deepDives.body:
Recalculating every formula on each edit is O(all formulas); a real sheet must touch only what changed.

**Graph:** for every formula cell, `precedents` are the cells it reads; the inverse, `dependents`, answers "who must update when this cell changes?".

```ts
const dependents = new Map<CellId, Set<CellId>>();

function setFormula(cell: CellId, refs: CellId[]) {
  for (const p of precedents.get(cell) ?? []) dependents.get(p)?.delete(cell);  // drop old edges
  precedents.set(cell, new Set(refs));
  for (const p of refs) (dependents.get(p) ?? dependents.set(p, new Set()).get(p)!).add(cell);
}
```

**Recalculate after an edit:**
1. Collect the dirty set: all transitive dependents of the changed cells (BFS over `dependents`).
2. Topologically sort the dirty set with **Kahn's algorithm**: count in-degrees restricted to dirty cells, start from zero in-degree, pop, evaluate, decrement neighbours.
3. Any dirty cells never reaching zero in-degree are on (or downstream of) a **cycle**; mark them `#CYCLE!` instead of looping forever.

```text
A1 = 5   B1 = A1*2   C1 = A1+B1      edit A1
dirty {B1, C1}; in-degree within dirty: B1=0, C1=1 (from B1)
order: B1 -> C1
```

**Ranges:** `=SUM(A1:A10000)` would add 10,000 edges. Store range dependencies separately (a list or interval index of ranges per formula) and, when a cell changes, also find formulas whose ranges contain it. This keeps memory linear in formulas, not in referenced cells.

**Volatile functions** (`NOW`, `RAND`) are marked dirty on every recalculation.

**Benchmark for the README:** a chain of 10,000 dependent cells, a fan-out of one cell to 10,000 formulas, and a 100k-cell sheet edit, each with measured recalculation time in the worker.

deepDives.title: Running the engine in a Web Worker
deepDives.body:
Recalculating thousands of cells or parsing a 20 MB CSV can take hundreds of milliseconds. On the main thread that is a long task: typing lags and scrolling freezes, which shows up directly in INP. A dedicated worker owns the engine so the UI thread only renders.

**Protocol (keep it small and typed):**

```ts
type ToWorker =
  | { type: "load"; cells: [CellId, string][] }
  | { type: "set"; seq: number; changes: { id: CellId; raw: string }[] }
  | { type: "importCsv"; text: string; at: CellId };

type FromWorker =
  | { type: "values"; seq: number; updates: [CellId, CellValue][] }
  | { type: "error"; message: string };
```

- The worker holds raw formulas, ASTs, the graph and values. The main thread keeps a mirror of displayed values only.
- Send **only changed cells** back, never the whole sheet.
- A `seq` number lets the UI ignore results from superseded edits and show a "calculating" hint while the latest seq is pending.
- On the main thread, apply incoming updates in one batch per animation frame so a large recalculation produces one render.

**Optimistic display:** when the user types a plain value, show it immediately; formulas show their previous value (or a subtle pending style) until the worker replies.

**Data transfer:** structured cloning copies data; for large numeric blocks, use ArrayBuffers and transfer them (zero-copy). Comlink can wrap the worker in an RPC-style API, but a plain discriminated-union protocol is easy to test and explain.

**Testing:** the engine is pure TypeScript with no DOM, so it runs in Vitest directly; the worker file is a thin adapter around it.

deepDives.title: 2D virtualisation and frozen panes
deepDives.body:
100,000 rows x 26 columns is 2.6 million cells; the grid must render only what is visible.

**One scroll container, one big spacer:**

```text
div.viewport (overflow: auto)
  div.spacer (height = rows * rowH, width = sum of column widths, position: relative)
    header cells   position: sticky; top: 0
    row numbers    position: sticky; left: 0
    visible cells  position: absolute; transform: translate(x, y)
```

`position: sticky` inside the same scroller keeps headers and row numbers aligned without any JavaScript scroll syncing, which would lag a frame behind.

**Visible window:**

```ts
const r0 = Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / ROW_H) - 3);
const r1 = Math.min(ROWS - 1, Math.ceil((scrollTop + height) / ROW_H) + 3);
// columns have variable widths: prefix sums + binary search
const c0 = lowerBound(colOffsets, scrollLeft) - 1;
```

TanStack Virtual supports a row virtualiser and a column virtualiser on the same element, which is a solid base; writing it by hand once is worth it for the interview story.

**Rendering cost:** render cells as lightweight memoised components keyed by position, read values with a per-cell selector so a recalculation re-renders only changed visible cells, and avoid context providers per cell.

**Focus and accessibility:** when keyboard navigation moves past the rendered window, scroll first, wait for the render, then focus the cell. `aria-rowcount`, `aria-colcount`, `aria-rowindex` and `aria-colindex` describe the full grid to screen readers.

**Limits:** browsers cap element heights (in the tens of millions of pixels), so beyond roughly a million rows you need scaled scrolling or a canvas renderer, which is the main stretch goal.
